answer.text: Only a single moving average line
A middle band (SMA) with upper and lower bands set at standard deviations from the SMA
Two parallel horizontal lines at fixed prices

explanation.text: The Logic: In standard technical-analysis usage, Bollinger Bands are a three-line volatility indicator: a middle band that is a simple moving average (commonly 20-period), and an upper and lower band plotted at a fixed number of standard deviations (commonly two) above and below the middle SMA. Because the bands are computed from rolling standard deviation, they widen when volatility rises and contract when it falls, which is the feature that distinguishes them from fixed horizontal price levels. The Trap: A single moving-average line describes a basic MA, not Bollinger Bands. Fixed horizontal lines describe static support/resistance, not a volatility envelope. "Only support and resistance levels" confuses Bollinger Bands with classical chart levels — the bands are dynamic and recompute each period. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook lists Bollinger Bands among technical indicators but does not, on the pages checked, define the middle/upper/lower band construction or specify a 20-period SMA with standard-deviation bands. The construction described above is general technical-analysis knowledge included for completeness.
